# Notes for the Next Owners

The realtor told me not to leave this. She said buyers want a blank slate, that a letter from the previous owner feels like a ghost standing in the kitchen. I'm leaving it anyway, in the drawer under the phone jack that no longer connects to anything. If you've found it, you're the kind of person who opens drawers, and I trust you already.

First, practical matters.

The third stair from the bottom creaks. Not the second, not the fourth. The third. You can step over it if you're trying to come home quietly, which my son learned at sixteen and which I pretended not to know for two years. The fourth stair also creaks, but only in winter, when the wood contracts. It sounds like someone saying "hm" in disagreement. You'll get used to it.

The kitchen window sticks in August. Don't force it. Take a butter knife and run it along the left side of the frame, where the paint has built up over forty years of people like me thinking one more coat would solve things. It won't. But the butter knife will.

There's a fig tree in the backyard that doesn't produce figs. I want to be honest about this because the listing described it as "a mature fig tree," which is technically true in the way that describing me as "a mature woman" is technically true. It has not given fruit since 1994. My husband believed it was waiting for something. He talked to it every spring, not in a whimsical way but in a stern, managerial way, like a foreman addressing a union holdout. It never gave in. I admired it for that, eventually.

You may cut it down. I would understand. But I'd ask you to give it one more spring. Not for sentimental reasons. I just have a feeling.

The basement floods when it rains more than two inches in a day. There's a sump pump. It works. It makes a sound like a large animal clearing its throat, and the first time you hear it at three in the morning you will sit bolt upright and wonder who is in your house. Nobody is in your house. It's just the pump, doing its job, being dramatic about it.

Now the less practical matters.

On the inside of the pantry doorframe there are pencil marks. Two children, measured every birthday from ages two to fourteen, and then, in different handwriting, two grandchildren measured on the occasional Thanksgiving. The lines are labeled with initials and dates. The highest one says *R, 14, finally taller than Mom*, and there's a small arrow pointing to a line slightly lower that says *Mom*, and next to that my own note: *temporarily*.

I know you'll paint over them. The realtor said I should do it myself before the showings, and I stood there with the brush for a while and then went and had a sandwich instead. I'm not asking you to preserve them. That would be unfair, like leaving you a pet you didn't agree to feed. I only want you to know what's under the paint, so that when you're standing in the pantry some night looking for the peanut butter, you might feel, without knowing why, that you are standing somewhere people grew.

And then, if you have children, I hope you'll start your own lines. There's room. The wood is good oak and takes a pencil well.

The bedroom at the end of the hall gets the best light in the house, between seven and eight in the morning. It comes in low and gold and lands on the wall opposite the window, and for about fifteen minutes the whole room looks like the inside of a peach. We used it as a guest room for years, which is a crime I can't undo. Sleep there. Or read there. Or just go in with your coffee and stand around. It's the only thing in the house I'd call magic, and it costs nothing, and it happens every clear day whether anyone is watching or not.

I've been thinking about that a lot lately, how much of what's beautiful just goes on without an audience. Every morning for twenty-some years that light filled that room and mostly nobody saw it. It didn't seem to mind.

A few more things.

The neighbor to the east, Dolores, will bring you a loaf of zucchini bread within your first week. It will be dense enough to use as a doorstop. Eat it anyway and tell her it's wonderful. She is eighty-one and has buried two husbands and a daughter, and the bread is how she says she's still here. You'll figure out what to say back.

The neighbor to the west has a dog named Pickles who barks at the mail carrier with a hatred that seems personal. There's no history there. Pickles just has convictions.

The hall closet has a light switch on the outside that turns on a light inside, but also, for reasons no electrician has ever explained, the porch light. You cannot have one without the other. My husband called it "the house's opinion" and stopped trying to fix it. I'd recommend the same approach to most of the house's opinions.

I'm moving somewhere smaller, closer to my daughter, with an elevator and a woman at the front desk who already knows my name. It's the right decision. I made it myself and I'd make it again. But I walked through every room this morning and touched the doorframes the way you'd touch someone's shoulder on the way past, and I want you to know that the house knows how to be lived in. It's good at it. It's had practice.

Be happy here. Be ordinary here, which is harder and better. Fight in the kitchen and make up in the kitchen, since that's where it always happens anyway. Let the stairs creak.

And watch the fig tree this spring.

I have a feeling.

— M.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering a few ideas for an open creative prompt—a lighthouse keeper's inventory, a clock repairer, a cartographer measuring distances in his late wife's house—but I'm leaning toward something fresher: a night-shift worker at a 24-hour laundromat who reads people's forgotten items.

Actually, I like the idea of "Notes for the Next Owners"—a letter to whoever buys the narrator's house, written in second person with domestic, specific details. I want to draft it with concrete touches: the creaky third stair, the window that sticks in August, the fig tree, pencil marks on the pantry doorframe marking children's heights. The narrator is elderly, moving to a smaller place after losing a spouse, and I want the tone to balance humor and grief without tipping into sentimentality, landing on a strong ending around 1000 words.
